problem: Existing multi-object search (MOS) methods (POMDP planners and DRL) explore inefficiently, lack semantic modeling and generalize poorly (sim-to-real). VLM-based single-object search methods cannot track multiple targets at once and use only coarse scene-level embeddings.
motivation: Robots in warehouses, homes and search-and-rescue must find several objects while minimizing travel. Common-sense knowledge in VLMs can guide exploration, but it needs multi-target tracking and fine-grained object-level co-occurrence cues in object-dense scenes.
key_idea: Finder builds multi-channel per-target score maps that fuse scene-to-object (BLIP-2 image-text similarity) and object-to-object (text-embedding co-occurrence weighted semantic map) correlations to pick frontiers for zero-shot multi-object search.
insight: Both correlation types matter: the ablation shows removing StO drops SR from 63.4% to 61.5% and removing OtO drops it to 58.3% (MSPL 0.389 to 0.364 / 0.337), so object-level co-occurrence is the more important cue. The gain over VLFM (32.4% SR), which uses only coarse scene-level scores, suggests fine-grained object-level cues are what improve exploration in object-dense scenes. Note the baselines were adapted to MOS by sequential target prompts, so part of the gap comes from multi-target tracking.
method: Object Detector: YOLOv7 for COCO classes and Grounding DINO for open-vocabulary objects; MobileSAM produces masks; a detected target's closest point is projected to 3D as a waypoint.
Spatial Map Generator: builds an occupancy map from depth and odometry and a semantic map of scene objects (following Chaplot et al.).

Scene-to-Object score map: BLIP-2 ITM cosine similarity between the RGB image and each target, scaled by a cone-shaped FOV confidence mask and updated with a confidence-weighted average, following VLFM; one channel per target.
Object-to-Object score map: co-occurrence matrix from Q-Former embedding cosine similarity between scene-object and target names, weighting each semantic-map channel and summing per target.
Score Fusion: min-max normalize each per-target channel, add StO and OtO element-wise, and sum over targets into one unified map (equal target priority).

Exploration Planner: picks the highest-scoring frontier; when a target is detected, goes to its waypoint using a pretrained VER point-goal policy (discrete actions). A target within threshold ε is removed from the list, and the robot stops when the list is empty.

setting.backbone: BLIP-2 (frozen), YOLOv7, Grounding DINO, MobileSAM, VER PointNav policy (pretrained, from VLFM)
setting.action_space: low-level discrete: move forward, turn left, turn right, stop (real robot: A* + TEB local planner velocities)

numbers.eval_set_note: 1000 episodes, 3 target objects per episode, 500-step limit

numbers_note: The paper gives no official split names for HM3D/MP3D, so 'val' is used. A Finder w/o StO ablation (SR 61.5, MSPL 0.364) is also reported but not listed. Real-world results are qualitative only.
results: Finder reaches 63.4% SR / 0.389 MSPL on HM3D and 55.4% / 0.344 on MP3D, beating VLFM (32.4% / 0.155 on HM3D, 12.6% / 0.104 on MP3D), L3MVN, CoW and MultiON (23.9% SR on MP3D), with Wilcoxon-significant gains. Exploration time saturates at about 300 steps as targets grow from 1 to 8, and the method also works on a real TurtleBot2 in a 121.5 m² building.
limitations: Relies on accurate object detection, static indoor environments, and high-performance compute (models run on an RTX 4090 desktop over the network, ~400 ms latency)
